items.title: Kioxia unveils E1.L SSDs for hyperscalers with up to 122.88TB capacity
units: Kioxia introduced its LD4-series solid-state drives (SSDs) in an E1.L form factor with capacities up to 122.88TB designed for high-density storage deployments in hyperscale data centers on Friday.

Kioxia's LD4-series SSDs rely on the company's proprietary platform complying with the NVMe 2.0e specification and featuring a single-port configuration along with select requirements of the Open Compute Project Datacenter NVMe SSD specification 2.6.

The key selling point of Kioxia's LD4-series and its E1.L form factor — 318.75 mm length × 38.4 mm height × 9.5 mm thick — is its ability to house numerous 3D NAND flash packages on an elongated printed circuit board, thus enabling multiple drives to be installed in a thin 1U server, offering vast capacities.

Kioxia is currently sampling 15.36 TB and 30.72 TB LD4 drives to select customers.

Although Kioxia lists PCIe 5.0 compliance, the drives operate at PCIe 4.0 x4 speeds of up to 16 GT/s per lane, which provides a theoretical maximum bandwidth of approximately 7.88 GB/s in each direction.
The new drives use proven BiCS8 3D QLC NAND and are aimed at read-intensive workloads like AI data repositories and object storage, according to the manufacturer.

While the company currently offers capacities of up to 30.72 TB, it has validated an architecture capable of supporting 122.88 TB drives, though it never revealed when such drives are set to be available, something not surprising in a world where 3D NAND memory is sold in advance.

items.title: Building Spyre as a Native PyTorch Device
units: Home » Blog » Building Spyre as a Native PyTorch Device Spyre becomes a native PyTorch device by connecting PyTorch’s existing device, allocator, stream, and compiler abstractions through torch-spyre to the Spyre runtime and firmware.

For Spyre, that means mapping PyTorch’s device, allocator, stream, event, and launch abstractions onto a runtime built around compiled programs, ordered queues, explicit data movement, and fixed layout contracts.
An ordinary PyTorch value was not simply a device="spyre" tensor whose storage PyTorch managed and whose allocation could be reused by the next operation.

PrivateUse1 gives Spyre a real device identity, PyTorch allocator storage keeps tensors resident on device="spyre", streams provide familiar ordering semantics, and runtime events connect dependent work across streams.
A native PyTorch device still has to honor the execution model of the hardware underneath it.
Torch-spyre provides the PyTorch device integration, while the Spyre runtime and firmware manage device work and communication.
Tensor lifetime becomes the framework’s problem: when the last reference to a Spyre tensor goes away, PyTorch calls back into the backend allocator to release or recycle the device allocation.

For Spyre, the useful mapping is not that the hardware behaves exactly like a PyTorch stream; it is that stream-ordered work can be lowered into typed runtime operations while the runtime preserves the dependencies those operations require.
As a consequence, PyTorch believed every tensor was a CPU tensor, even if the core runtime had really moved it to the device.
A tensor on device="spyre" needs real device storage whose lifetime PyTorch owns through its allocator and storage contracts.

On Spyre, the framework-facing layer turns the compiled artifact into a prepared launch plan: a recipe that records the host work, data movement, device compute, and synchronization needed to run that artifact.
The result is one path for eager and compiled execution, lower launch overhead, and a PyTorch surface that maps cleanly onto Spyre’s hardware.

items.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
units: The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox.
Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone.

Later, when researchers tested them on specific tasks, like trying to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak, the agents that had spent 30 hours playing on the island performed better than fresh copies without the same experience.
Norelli highlights an example where Eko started juggling and set a record of 50 consecutive catches.

Another iteration of Eko started making up its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” where it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground.
Eko then decided that the catches had happened too quickly to really count, so it canceled its record and started again with stricter rules.

Although Eko was not explicitly instructed to invent games or explore the island, it did have a master prompt in the form of a “soul” file, a text document that described it as “naturally curious” and eager to explore.
“It’s an artifact that learned from our culture, was trained by engineers at Anthropic, and was then placed on an island by us,” he says.
“It’s not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play,” says Phillip Isola, an MIT professor and a coauthor of the paper.
Ultimately, the question of whether AI agents are actually playing or just imitating play may not actually matter.
“Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” wrote this version of Eko in its activity log.

items.title: Inside Prometheus: Meta’s Journey to a Gigawatt-Scale Supercluster
units: The Prometheus supercluster is housed in Meta’s New Albany, Ohio, data center.
Both DSF and NSF are based on Meta’s FBOSS networking stack, giving us the control to rapidly iterate on and optimize the fabrics in Prometheus, and the visibility to operate these clusters at scale.
NVIDIA’s next-generation Vera Rubin NVL72 platform will be a generational leap in per-GPU performance and will integrate directly into Prometheus’s existing network fabric.
Right now, in New Albany, Ohio, Meta is undertaking its most ambitious AI infrastructure project to date.

Running pretraining over this network required a dedicated optimization effort with Meta Superintelligence Labs to ensure training was not slowed down, especially given speed-of-light constraints at these distances.
While Meta optimizes scheduling and infrastructure, NVIDIA addresses firmware, signal diagnostics, and memory handling.
Meta’s newest AI-optimized data centers use closed-looped, liquid cooling as it is the most efficient way to cool GPU servers, and supports efficient use of water.
At full scale, Prometheus will comprise roughly 1 million distributed GPUs, all functioning in lockstep.
Prometheus currently deploys two NVIDIA GPU platforms, with a third (based on NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 ) arriving soon.
The Backend Aggregation (BAG) network is a multi-layer hub-and-spoke network that connects building-level fabrics across the Prometheus cluster, spanning 2 km to over 100 km.

Pulling this all together, the complexity of the Prometheus network involves millions of miles of fiber strand, tens of thousands of switches, and millions of optics — from 2×400G FR4 LITE short-reach, low-cost pluggables inside the buildings to 800G-ZR coherent optics for links beyond ~10 km.
Maintaining reliability at this level requires a co-engineering model with NVIDIA that goes beyond a traditional vendor dynamic.

items.title: Unpatched Broadcom Wi-Fi Flaw Lets Attackers in Range Run Code as Root on Routers
units: A flaw in Broadcom's Wi-Fi setup software lets an attacker within radio range run code as root on Broadcom-based routers, without the network password or any pairing step, security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed on October 16.
The flaw is in Broadcom's version of Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS), the feature that lets a device join a Wi-Fi network without the password being typed in.

Kaiser traces the code back to at least 2010 and says Broadcom shipped an incomplete fix in 2018, then told customers to switch to a different Wi-Fi software package, called hostapd, rather than relying on the fix.
Broadcom's WPS code is embedded in routers and access points from dozens of vendors, and Kaiser estimates that millions of devices worldwide are affected.
Broadcom's code mishandles the reassembly of fragmented WPS setup messages, so an attacker in range can send crafted messages that corrupt the router's memory.
Kaiser frames the bug as well suited to attackers who reach a target over nearby Wi-Fi rather than the internet, a technique Russian state hackers have used to breach networks from across the street.

Kaiser says Broadcom told him it has known about the bug since 2018 and had heard about it from others, but would not register a CVE or say anything publicly, which he believes is why so many device makers never patched.
From there, Kaiser built two things: a way to read memory back off the device, and a way to run his own code on it.
When he took the case to the CERT Coordination Center, it was closed the same day, because Broadcom itself holds the authority to assign CVEs for its products and would not do so.
Against a Proximus gateway, the Sagemcom-built BBOX3V+, the exploit opened a reverse shell, a remote command line, carried over Wi-Fi frames, so no outside server was needed.
In Belgium, Kaiser found the flaw present and exploitable on gateways from three of the four big providers: Proximus, Orange Belgium and VOO.
Both ran without any login, and the attack works at a distance, not only up close, Kaiser says.

units: Town, a two-year-old, San Francisco-based startup developing AI assistants, nabbed a unicorn valuation on Monday, announcing a $108 million Series B funding round co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures.
Town — founded by former Plaid CTO Jean-Denis Greze — is one of many AI assistants flooding the market right now.
Town targets businesses, giving each employee an AI assistant called a Townie that helps with tasks by connecting to tools such as emails and calendars, as well as other core work systems.

items.title: WhatsApp Help Pages Leaked Hidden Instructions for a Meta Chatbot
units: A new analysis has found that around 80 help and FAQ pages across WhatsApp’s website exposed text instructions that were designed for a large language model, specifically one of Meta’s own.
Dozens of WhatsApp web pages designed to answer people’s questions about Meta’s encrypted messaging app inadvertently exposed the company’s own instructions to its chatbot.

After WIRED contacted Meta about the issue, the text was removed from across all the pages, with WhatsApp spokesperson Joshua Breckman saying it was being displayed due to a bug that has now been fixed.
The instructions, according to findings from privacy company Redact, appeared in the webpages’ code and contained written details that were not explicitly on the WhatsApp help pages.

“These are instructions to our chatbot, not directly to users, and are intended to ensure accurate and relevant responses for WhatsApp users who choose to message WhatsApp Support with AI,” Breckman says.

“Do not cite, quote, interpret, or reference WhatsApp Terms of Service, Privacy Policy, or any legal document,” the instructions said, adding not to make any statements about WhatsApp liability or non-liability.
WIRED viewed the exposed text, which can still be seen when viewing the underlying code of archived versions of the help pages.

Among the 100 blocks of hidden text, the directions appeared to provide guidance to steer an LLM from answering users questions in unhelpful ways and provide a glimpse at how instructions for chatbots are created.
Breckman, the WhatsApp spokesperson, says that the company provides users with transparent information about their data rights and how they can take actions.
“We want our product support chatbots to be focused on providing the best advice to users about WhatsApp—not to offer legal advice,” Breckman says.

He says the company regularly scans the sites and privacy policies of big tech firms, and that many of the WhatsApp instructions the team found were straightforward and point people towards other official support channels.
Still, it does not appear the instructions were meant for public exposure.
items.whatHappened: Around 80 pages on WhatsApp’s website exposed instructions that were designed for its chatbot, including “WHAT NOT TO SAY.”
